results.title: Investigation of the structure and magnitude of time-varying uncontrolled confounding in simulated cohort data analyzed using g-computation
results.content: Complex DAGs that included relationships between uncontrolled confounders and other variables and relationships where exposures caused uncontrolled confounders at the next time point resulted in the most biased effect estimates. Seminal works have developed methods for modelling time-varying exposures, outcomes and confounders when evaluating longitudinal observational studies.1,2 In these studies, current measurements are affected by prior measurements and conventional regression can inadvertently bias results.3 Robins’ generalized methods (g-methods) addresses these complexities through the fitting of marginal structural models with inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) or the g-computation algorithm to estimate time-varying effects.3 Thus, there has been a proliferation in tutorials with various statistical software and their application in research.3–5 Whereas IPTW has been widely used, g-computation (g-formula) or a generalization of standardization in a single time point study has recently increased in use. Thus, this paper seeks to describe structures of time-varying uncontrolled confounding using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and to demonstrate the impact of time-varying uncontrolled confounding on effect estimates obtained from g-computation in data simulated to resemble cohort study settings. We use the following notation to describe the relationships between our time-varying exposures or treatments (X t), measured and sufficient set of confounders (Z t), outcome (Y), and uncontrolled confounders (U t) over multiple time points, indexed by the subscript _t_ (1–4). Finally, the most complex structure builds upon DAG D and includes the relationship between the uncontrolled confounders at time t and t + 1, and the exposure causes the next uncontrolled confounder [Supplementary Figure S1E (DAG E), available as Supplementary data at _IJE_ online: X t←U t→Y, X t+1, Z t, U t+1 and X t→U t+1]. In the presence of time-varying uncontrolled confounding, relationships of the uncontrolled confounders with other variables are present in the post-intervention DAGs (Figure 2A and B and Supplementary Figure S2 (available as Supplementary data at _IJE_ online) for DAGs 1–2 and A–E, respectively). To demonstrate the impact of time-varying uncontrolled confounding, we simulated data representing the pre-intervention DAGs 1–2 and A–E. We observed that the presence of multiple time-varying uncontrolled confoundering relationships resulted in a larger biased estimate in our simulated models.

Being accepted as a legitimate organization by stakeholders could equip MNCs with better access to resources (e.g., financial and reputation capital, and government support) which could ultimately enhance company growth and survival (Cruz-Suarez et al., 2014;Tost, 2011;Zimmerman & Zeitz, 2002). This study aimed to contribute to emerging market CSR literature by examining the relationship between CSR engagement and corporate performance of Chinese manufacturing MNCs operating in Africa, with emphasis on moral legitimacy as a mediating factor and institutional distance as a moderating factor. Literature distinguishes between three main types of organizational legitimacy, namely, pragmatic, moral, and cognitive legitimacy [15,[17][18][19][20]. This study examined the relationship between Chinese manufacturing MNCs’ engagement in terms of CSR and gaining moral legitimacy in host countries, and whether the institutional distance between countries is an important moderating factor in this relationship. Since cognitive legitimacy holds an important position in corporate management decisions [14], and environmental information disclosure is a crucial means for companies to gain legitimacy [15], publicly disclosing corporate social responsibility reports and other information can effectively enhance legitimacy [16] [17] [18] [19] [20], especially for companies in environmentally sensitive industries. This paper analyzes a multidimensional model of organizational legitimacy, competencies, and resources in order to develop the linkage between institutional and resource-based perspectives by systematically detailing relationships among these factors and organizational viability. This article relates institutional theory to the concept of organizational legitimacy with cognitive, moral, and pragmatic dimensions, to analyse how a Dutch national policy reform – aimed at expanding the social responsibility for sick leave and disability toward non-state organizations – is understood and enacted locally.
